maps.title: A court draws its beginnings
maps.subtitle: Compare Jimmu’s traditional route to Nara with the archaeological centers.
maps.caption: The court’s story goes east by the Inland Sea and approaches the Nara basin after a detour. Izumo and early Nara have archaeological histories visible independently of the story.

timeline.label: Late Pleistocene
timeline.caption: The climatic parent horizon includes the colder landscapes and changing sea levels within which Paleolithic settlement developed.

timeline.label: Upper Paleolithic in Japan
timeline.caption: A widespread and secure archaeological record is visible by roughly 38,000 years ago; local sequences and end dates vary.

timeline.label: Last Glacial Maximum
timeline.caption: Peak glacial conditions provide the environmental contrast for later warming, forest expansion, and changing mobility.

timeline.label: Incipient Jomon (Mesolithic transition)
timeline.caption: Pottery and changing lifeways overlap the late-glacial transition; the phase is archaeological, not a single archipelago-wide revolution.

timeline.label: Early Holocene
timeline.caption: Rapid warming, rising seas, and expanding temperate forests transformed the resource landscape after the Pleistocene.

timeline.label: Early Jomon
timeline.caption: Marine transgression and increasingly substantial settlements frame the Early Jomon in many regions.

timeline.label: Middle Jomon
timeline.caption: Large highland settlements and elaborate material traditions flourished especially in central and eastern Honshu.

timeline.label: Late Jomon
timeline.caption: Settlement and ritual landscapes shifted after the Middle Jomon florescence, with strong regional variation.

timeline.label: Final Jomon
timeline.caption: This broad framework is not a uniform end date: farming began earlier in northern Kyushu while Jomon traditions continued elsewhere.

timeline.label: Initial and Early Yayoi (northern Kyushu)
timeline.caption: Wet-rice farming began in northern Kyushu in the tenth to ninth centuries BC; the transition reached other regions later.

timeline.label: Itazuke early paddy horizon
timeline.caption: The earliest farming horizon is placed within northern Kyushu's long Jomon–Yayoi transition; exact site phases remain debated.

timeline.label: Middle Yayoi
timeline.caption: Agriculture, continental exchange, metallurgy, and new burial forms expanded unevenly across western and central Japan.

timeline.label: Late Yayoi
timeline.caption: Regional centers, defended settlements, bronze ritual systems, and the polities described in Chinese records belong to this broad horizon.

timeline.label: Early Kofun horizon
timeline.caption: Standardized monumental keyhole tombs spread from the mid-third century and mark a new scale of political integration.

timeline.label: Kojindani bronze deposition horizon
timeline.display_date: ca. first century BC–first century AD
timeline.caption: Swords were found in one deposit, and bells and spearheads in another seven metres away. The dates of deposition are uncertain.

timeline.label: Himiko's rule in Yamatai
timeline.caption: The Wei account names Himiko and describes her rule before her reported death around AD 248. The beginning of her rule is particularly uncertain.

timeline.label: Wei replies to Himiko’s first embassy
timeline.caption: The Wei court recognized Himiko and sent titles and gifts. The chronology is commonly given as AD 238 or 239.

timeline.label: Reported death of Himiko
timeline.caption: The account associates her death with renewed disorder and a large burial mound.

timeline.label: Earliest monumental keyhole mounds in the Nara basin
timeline.caption: Large mounds belong to the third-to-fourth-century transition. A mound’s date does not establish the name of its occupant.

timeline.label: Eastern Han
timeline.caption: Eastern Han sources contain early written notices of Wa and its envoys.

timeline.label: King of Na in Wa receives a Han seal
timeline.caption: The Later Han record provides an early fixed point for diplomatic contact with a polity in Wa.

timeline.label: Cao Wei dynasty
timeline.caption: Himiko's diplomacy was conducted with the Wei court during China's Three Kingdoms period.

timeline.label: Claimed first reign of Jimmu
timeline.caption: The later imperial chronology dates the legendary beginning to 660 BC. The itinerary does not establish a historical campaign in that year.

timeline.label: Kojiki completed
timeline.caption: The surviving court narrative was compiled many centuries after the world it retrospectively orders.

timeline.label: Nihon Shoki completed
timeline.caption: The official chronicle was presented in 720 and constructed a continuous dynastic past.

paragraphs.text: In 1946, at Iwajuku in central Honshu, Aizawa Tadahiro found a flake of black stone in the exposed red earth beside a road. The fragment was obsidian, a glass formed in volcanic rock, and its edge had been made by a blow. What mattered as much as the stone was where it lay. If tools really came from earth older than the layers that held Jomon pottery, then the pots with their cord marks lay somewhere in the middle of the human story. In 1949, excavation confirmed what the flake had given Aizawa reason to suspect.

There is a difference between picking up a stone and finding one in a layer. A stone in the hand can tell you something about the blow that made it. A stone still in the bank can tell you which earth covered it, and which earth had yet to fall. Across the Kanto plain, ash from successive eruptions settled over the surfaces on which people had made their fires and struck their tools. The ash that once fell on a place where people lived is part of the reason we can tell one occupation from another. The better dated sites now put people in the archipelago roughly thirty-eight thousand years ago. The famous claims for far older occupations at Zazaragi and Babadan collapsed when the supposed evidence was exposed as planted.

Ice lay on the highest mountains. Across much of the rest of the archipelago, the cold changed the forests without covering the land with glaciers. Mammoths reached Hokkaido from the north. At Lake Nojiri in central Honshu, bones and teeth preserve a different world of great deer and Naumann elephants. The breadth of the seas changed as well. A colder world kept more water in ice, exposing what are now submerged coastal plains. The northern shelf towards Sakhalin offered different possibilities from the southern passages near the Korean peninsula and the Ryukyu islands. Some crossings narrowed without closing. A map of modern Japan gives the distances between the islands today. For the first people to move through this country, some of the shores were elsewhere.

Beside a stream on the Kanto plain you could gather cobbles and make a serviceable edge. Some of the people who camped along the Nogawa nevertheless used obsidian whose source lay well over a hundred kilometres away in the mountains of central Honshu. They used glass from Hakone too, closer to the plain but still a long walk away. The stone carries something of its birthplace in its chemistry. That is how we can know where an edge began even when there is no way to know how many hands brought it to the camp. The distance is real whether someone went to collect the stone, received it on the way home, or acquired it from strangers.

Obsidian from Kozushima sets a harder problem. This little volcanic island off the Izu Peninsula was separated from Honshu by water even when the sea was lower. People on Honshu were using stone sourced to the island in the Paleolithic. However the pieces travelled after landing, at least one part of their passage was across open water. A pale line on a map can join the island to the coast in a second. The stone on the mainland is the trace of the decision to take it out to sea. The craft itself has vanished.

The camp on the plain is sometimes easier to picture than the crossing. Alongside the flakes are clusters of stones from river gravel, some blackened, reddened or cracked by heat. They are evidence of cooking, a part of life that a beautifully shaped projectile point scarcely suggests. As the forests changed and some large animals disappeared, hunters and gatherers had a different range of foods to work with. At the Kamikuroiwa shelter in Shikoku, older layers hold spearpoints and large game bones. Higher up lie small arrowheads, with the bones of birds and smaller animals among the remains. The size of an edge changed along with the animals brought back to the shelter.

A fired clay pot can sit over a fire long enough to cook what it holds. The clay has to survive drying, firing and then the heat of a fire again. Some of the earliest vessels in the archipelago were simply shaped and decorated with a few raised or impressed marks. Fragments survive in the north, including at Odai Yamamoto in Aomori, as well as in caves in Kyushu. There are older finds on the Asian mainland. On some of the ancient fragments from the archipelago, a dark crust still adheres to the interior. Its chemistry points to the cooking of fish and other aquatic foods. We can recover something of the contents of a pot whose maker lived thousands of years before anyone planted rice there.

Shells tell another part of the story. At Natsushima, near what is now Tokyo Bay, oysters and warm-water clams accumulated where people ate. Different layers hold different mixtures of freshwater and marine remains as the sea came farther in. In parts of the Kanto plain a shell mound can now lie well inland. Walk what looks today like dry country and you are crossing ground that once lay beside a tidal inlet. There was loss in this too. People could move up to a bluff above the new water. Whatever they left on lower ground was liable to disappear from the record almost as completely as it disappeared from their lives.

At Hanawadai in Ibaraki, five hollows mark houses, though probably only two or three stood in use together. The posts have gone. The hearths were outside, and pointed pots could stand in soft soil that would have made a poor surface for a flat-bottomed one. There may have been ten or fifteen people here in all. A different kind of closeness comes from a man buried beneath shells at Hirasaka. His lower teeth had worn almost to the jaw on one side. His bones preserve interruptions in his childhood growth. Perhaps he repeatedly pulled a leather thong or some other material across those teeth. The wear is visible down to the root. The gesture that produced it is lost.

At Minanbori, a village above the water in present-day Yokohama, new houses kept facing the same open space as the old ones. The arrangement survived successive rebuildings. Roofs shed water into ditches, hearths moved indoors, and flat bases let pots stand on the hard floor. Some storage pits held nuts in layers separated by leaves, so only the topmost food had to be exposed when a household opened one. A roof and a hearth make a house habitable. A way of keeping food through the winter and a place the neighbors keep opening their doors onto give it a longer life.

At Torihama on the other side of Honshu, wet ground saved objects that normally disappear. A comb, rope and pieces of basketry survived beside wooden bows and oars and bowls. Much of what would have met your hand in a Jomon village would have been plant fibre, wood, bark or a lacquered surface. A dry site can leave nearly all of that out. Even the food refuse in the pots at Torihama reaches across millennia. Traces of cooking aquatic foods run through much of the long sequence of occupation. People returned to that resource as waters, woods and the rest of the diet changed.

The word Jomon means cord pattern. Rolled or pressed into soft clay, a cord leaves a trace of every turn of the fibre. The name, taken from pots at the Omori shell mounds, came to cover a great span of time and many ways of living. People on distant coasts could leave much the same marks in clay while living by very different means. Around the coast, fish, shellfish, game and nuts kept drawing people back to particular ground. In the central mountains, people were about to make surprisingly large settlements around some of the least tractable food on the list.

A horse chestnut is a poor thing to put straight into your mouth. So are many kinds of acorn. Both can sustain a household through winter if someone gathers enough and knows how to get the bitterness out. Running water could take much of the work, provided the water was close and someone had time to leave the nuts in it. This is one reason springs matter so much around the slopes of Yatsugatake. By about the middle of the fourth millennium BC, substantial villages grew in the central highlands near springs, woods and routes to workable stone. The height and the cold of winter make this seem a less inviting place to settle until you consider the food and water available in the same few miles.

A village could live by horse chestnuts ripening first, other nuts later, and roots and bulbs worked into food that would keep. At Idojiri, charred starchy pieces suggest something like bread. There were difficult judgments here which the broad word gathering tends to conceal. One tree yields what another will yield a few weeks later, and a poor crop changes how carefully you have to set aside what you have. People may have encouraged some plants to grow closer to home. The evidence allows for active tending and selection, though it leaves the character and extent of cultivation open. A permanent house and stored food were possible well before a rice field made them familiar.

At Yosukeone, near Togariishi, the hearth in a new house could be made with stones taken from a house a few metres away. Archaeologists could fit the stones to hollows they had left in older floors. Some standing stones and clay figures were also carried over. There is no record of the occasions that called for these short removals. A house might have worn out, or the people in it might have wanted to leave the place where an illness or a death had occurred. In either case, they had a choice about what to carry. More than two dozen house pits were found. When the settlement was finally abandoned, only five houses still had their hearthstones in place.

Clay also travelled through this district. Some lowland pots contained flakes of mica which catch the light. Mixed into the clay, the mica also made it more resistant to heat and less liable to shrink. Its sources were limited, so a pot far from them tells us that clay, vessels, or people who could make vessels travelled between the sources and the settlements. In the uplands, the rims of some pots rise into heavy reliefs, with animal heads and the bodies of snakes. We can follow the movement of the material more readily than the movement of the image. The snake winds around the rim where a hand would have held the vessel.

At Shakado, where the mountains come down into the Kofu basin, more than a thousand pieces of clay figures were recovered. Whole figures are conspicuously scarce. A bare arm or a torso may be all that remains. At Hiraide, most of the figures at the settlement came from one burned house set a little apart from the others. These things may have been handled in illness, childbirth, or other moments of danger. The find at each place gives a different sort of clue. At Shakado there is the repetition of breakage. At Hiraide there is the extraordinary concentration in one room. Neither clue tells us what was said in that room or at what point a figure had done what was asked of it.

In some settlements a large inverted pot covered the remains of a child. Some vessels used in such settings had lost their bases or had been pierced through them. There were also pots buried at house entrances, where archaeologists have considered uses ranging from the burial of an infant to the burial of a placenta. Everybody who came in or went out passed over the same small place. Beyond that, the customs differ and the things people meant by them are harder to retrieve. A pot made to stand in the middle of household work could end its use beneath a threshold.

The density of settlement in the highlands did not last. Around the transition to the Late Jomon, the counts of known sites fall steeply in parts of central Honshu. Some places lay empty while people and pottery traditions appear more widely in valleys, on coasts and in regions that had held fewer settlements. Poor nut harvests after wet seasons are one possible part of the explanation. The finds establish the change in settlement more firmly than a particular run of weather. Nor can every district be made to decline at the same rate. In the north, a different landscape of villages, cemeteries and craft was still taking shape.

A shell can carry the season of its death along its edge. Growth rings in shells left in some Late Jomon middens indicate long spells of collecting in spring, and sometimes another spell later in the summer. Other remains give the year a different shape in different places. The open sea could offer tuna and bonito to people who went out in dugout boats. Farther north there were salmon, and in autumn the woods had their own harvest. No one midden supplies a calendar for the whole archipelago. What it can give us is the trace of repeated visits to the same stretch of shore when the water was likely to yield something.

Burials were increasingly given ground of their own. At some sites people placed the dead with their legs drawn up, used red ochre, or left bracelets of shell and earrings of clay. At others they altered the teeth of the living. There are missing teeth where the surrounding bone healed after removal, and teeth filed to shapes they would never have taken by wear alone. The pattern can differ by age, by sex and from village to village. It may have marked stages of life or the relationships someone had entered. Whatever the rule, it could be made visible every time a person opened their mouth.

At Oyu, in what is now Akita, river stones were carried up to a terrace and laid out in two great rings. The larger circle is just over fifty metres across. Inside and around the rings are smaller arrangements of stones, some associated with pits interpreted as graves. Even the smaller circle is forty-four metres across, a distance made of separate loads carried up from the river. People may have come together here seasonally, and they may have returned when someone died. The site has room for more than one kind of gathering. It gives us the shape of repeated labor with a precision it cannot give us the words spoken there.

The places people returned to were also linked by materials that wore a more ordinary face. Bitumen from sources in Akita travelled across the northeast on pots that had been mended and on tools that needed fixing into their handles. Archaeologists have found more fishhooks at some coastal settlements than the people there seem to have needed for their own lines. Salt, dried seafood and shells could travel inland and stone could travel down to the shore. On one side of a mountain a broken pot can be repaired with a substance that came from the other.

In the later northern communities, the wet ground preserved lacquered bowls and combs at places like Korekawa. Lacquer can make a wooden object last longer in use. It can also make the smallest object arrest the eye. The fine polished surfaces and the red still visible on some of the pieces tell of a craft carried on long after many settlements in the central highlands had thinned out. The hollow clay figures of the northern Final Jomon have heavy eyes that have come to be called goggle eyes. The name describes what our own eyes see. The people who finished those faces left their handwork and took the meanings with them.

At the western end of the Inland Sea, another kind of surface was soon to keep the impression of something quite ordinary. While northern communities were still fitting long-established ways of making and obtaining food to their own country, water was being led over cleared ground in northern Kyushu. What would become an agricultural age entered the archipelago at one end. A family in the northeast could still polish a lacquered bowl of familiar shape while someone in the southwest was levelling a field for rice.

At Itazuke in northern Kyushu, a rice field preserved the prints of bare feet. Among the larger impressions excavators recognized the smaller prints of a child. The field had been drained before later soil covered it. At the same level were fragments of a kind of pot called Yusu, associated with the end of the Jomon sequence. For generations, pottery had supplied the boundary with the succeeding period, the Yayoi. Here feet had crossed a paddy while people were still using pots on the older side of that boundary. The surface that kept the print was wet enough to take the weight of a child.

Follow the coast north from Itazuke and the Korean peninsula comes into the story. Between it and Kyushu lie Tsushima and Iki. The islands break the passage into stages without removing the need to cross open sea. The first wet fields in northern Kyushu belong roughly around the beginning of the first millennium BC, with local dates still debated. Rice reached the archipelago through the peninsula, from a much longer history of cultivation on the continent. A cargo of grain could get someone through a winter. To get a crop in a new place required seed, a suitable bed, and people who understood when water had to enter and when it had to go.

Migrants had a part in bringing that knowledge. So did people already there, who put the new practices to work in places they knew and went on making familiar pots and gathering familiar foods. There was ample scope for both things to happen within the same village. An ancient genome from a burial at Doigahama, on the western tip of Honshu, carries ancestry related to Jomon populations and to migrants from the continent. A few people buried in northwestern Kyushu show differing amounts of such ancestry. Those lives bring a long change down to the scale of a few generations. In that time, people whose families had arrived by sea could leave descendants in the same burial ground as people with deeper roots nearby.

It took time for cultivation to make its way east. The Inland Sea offered one route, marked in part by the spread of pots of a kind first used in northern Kyushu. The paddies themselves had to be built one low patch at a time. Some communities combined dry fields and wet ones with hunting, fishing and the gathering of plants. Others kept older economies for much longer. A field and a pot travelled on different schedules. In parts of the northeast, farmers eventually planted rice and still made vessels in traditions that had outlasted the Jomon elsewhere. The fact that some Jomon villages had already stayed in place for generations makes the difference clearer. Rice made a new kind of staying possible, with a harvest that could be dried and kept in quantities, bound to carefully managed plots.

At Itazuke, wood survives in field stakes and implements. There is also a ditch and there are vessels large enough to store grain. The strip of land on which the inhabitants worked was beside the Mikasa River. The short journey from the fields towards the cemetery leads to a second kind of pottery, made to hold bodies. A child could fit inside a single jar. For an adult, two jars could be joined at the mouth. Earth presses on a vessel when it is buried, and in later northern Kyushu cemeteries people found different ways to set the jars so they would bear that weight. Some cemeteries eventually held hundreds of them.

Among the older uses of pots was sheltering the bodies of infants close to home. At Itazuke the dead had a larger, more clearly allotted ground away from the fields and stores. The footprints and the burials belong to different portions of the archaeological record. Their proximity still makes the settlement unusually legible. You can follow a stretch of ground from where people took care of what they would live on to where they chose to put their dead. Elsewhere the cemetery begins to show who could be set apart, and what could be placed in the ground with them.

At Toro, near the lower Abe River in what is now Shizuoka, the flood left pieces of timber lying the way the water had run. Beneath the flood deposits were house sites, raised stores and the divisions of a system of rice fields. Water had been the condition of the village. It could also erase the lines its people had spent years making. The inhabitants came back after an early flood and strengthened some of the ridges and channels with wooden boards and stakes. The repaired banks allow us to see both the damage and the decision to take the land back into use.

Look closely at the thin, regular wooden slats from the fields and paths. Few iron implements survived the damp ground. Their edges left marks in the timber they shaped. Iron reached the archipelago through continental connections and was gradually worked in local shops. A blade made finer, more repeatable cuts in wood. That mattered to a person fitting boards into a sluice, just as it mattered to someone shaping a hoe, a vessel or a part of a loom. In waterlogged sites we can sometimes follow the change from the tool to the work it made possible. At Toro the work has lasted longer than the edge that did it.

Some of the houses at Toro stood so near one another that there was scarcely room between them to dry their own grain. A raised storehouse could serve several houses. A cluster of wooden tools in one place suggests that at least some equipment was kept together. The fields were divided by banks, with smaller divisions inside larger ones. If a ditch filled with silt, whose turn was it to clear it? If a bank broke, the need for repair would occur at several doorways at once. The remains give us the repeated work that the neighbors had to arrange, even where the names of the people who arranged it have disappeared.

At Doigahama, west of the Inland Sea, most bodies lay outstretched, with their heads towards the east. A small group of stone-lined graves occupied the center of the cemetery. That group held jasper and shell ornaments seldom found in the rest of the cemetery. Closeness to the middle could have to do with rank, kinship or the history of the cemetery itself. Farther south in northern Kyushu, some graves held imported mirrors and other rare things in quantities most households could never have gathered. At Tateiwa, a man was buried with fourteen bracelets on his right arm. The shells came from warm waters far to the south. The fourteen bracelets still lay along the bones of his right arm.

At Santonodai, above what is now Yokohama, people lived on a plateau and grew rice down by springs on the slope. A ditch set off the settlement. Eight houses seem to have burned together. One of them was appreciably larger than the others and held large pots. Accident and attack can leave much the same burned floor. Other sites give a less equivocal kind of evidence. At Nejiko an arrowhead of bronze was found embedded in a woman's skull. At Yoshinogari there were bodies without heads. Something of the cost of making enemies survives even where the reasons and the names of the sides do not.

These villages could defend their high ground and still depend every day on work lower down. Land, water, supplies and passages mattered because people had put a great deal of their lives into them. The effort could draw households together, and it created things somebody else could seize. But the goods which came to distinguish a few graves depended on connections over much longer distances than a valley. In western Japan, some communities acquired enough of one costly material to take a remarkable further step. They took it out of circulation altogether and put it under a hill.

A small bronze bell with a clapper is made to be heard. Some early Yayoi bells were small enough to hang and shake. Their form recalls bells known on the Korean peninsula. In the archipelago, the form grew into objects too large and thin to work in the old way. Many later bells had no clapper. Raised bands and pierced flanges became conspicuous, and on some bells small figures appeared. Hunting with dogs, pounding rice, fish and raised storehouses could all be worked into the metal. At some point people were giving the bell a size and care that made sense for looking at it.

At Yasunagata, in northern Kyushu, a used bell mold came to light beside weapon molds and metalworking debris. The damaged surface of a poorly cast bell could be patched. Later casters managed to make larger bells with finer, cleaner detail. Matching products in settlements far apart show that the same mold, or the bells made from it, could travel. Foundries in the Kinki were important, but the finds in Kyushu show that bells were made there as well. The map records concentrations, with more weapons in parts of the west and more bells in parts of the east. Look between the two and you find exchange, shared shapes and places where the distinction will not hold.

Over time some bronze weapons became wider, thinner and less suited to use in someone's hand. They retained the shape of something a person could wield after they had lost much of its practicality. At Sakuragaoka, on a ridge above present-day Kobe, fourteen bells and seven halberds were found together. Their position above worked ground is like that of other deposits away from houses. Whether the metal was placed there to be used again at intervals, or given up entirely, is harder to establish. It helps to think of the weight before thinking of the ceremony. Somebody first had to get all that bronze to the hillside.

At Kojindani, on the Japan Sea side of western Honshu, a survey for a road led eventually to the excavation of three hundred and fifty-eight bronze swords. They were nearly the same length. They had been laid in four ordered rows in a cut in the slope. In two of those rows the points all faced east. A thin dark layer above them was taken as the possible trace of cloth. The following year six bells and sixteen spearheads came out of another deposit only seven metres away. The care in the alignment of the swords survives. What the distance between the two deposits meant to the people who made it is still open.

To lay down so much metal, a community first had to acquire it. Studies of the lead in some bells point to sources in Korea and China. Bronze could travel in finished objects, as metal for casting, or as scrap still worth the journey. A mirror might reach the archipelago intact. Metal that had been part of another object could go back into a crucible and come out in a shape unfamiliar to its first makers. There are limits to what a chemical comparison can follow through all that melting. But the halls and graveyards of the archipelago were connected to places across the water by repeated work and traffic.

For most of this history the people who carried the objects remain without names. In the third century AD, a delegation crossed those waters, and someone at a court in China wrote down the names of the leading envoys and the queen who had sent them. The court answered with gifts. Among them were a hundred bronze mirrors.

The queen's name was Himiko. She appears in a Chinese history of Wei which gives the people across the strait the collective name Wa. In the account, several countries had been at war for years before they agreed upon a ruler. Her seat is usually called Yamatai, a name preserved in Chinese writing. Once Himiko was made queen, very few people saw her. Armed men stood guard outside her residence. The account gives her numerous women attendants and one man who carried in food and carried words in and out. Her younger brother helped to govern. Whatever those inside the enclosure understood by her service to spirits, the writer understood that she could exercise authority through people who had very different degrees of access to her.

genealogy.caption: Himiko’s brother assisted her in government. The Wei account separately describes a man who brought food and passed messages.

paragraphs.text: The world outside the enclosure is visible in the same account. Markets traded in what one district had and another lacked. There were stores, dues and men for whom others had to step aside. When someone of lower standing met a man of rank on the road, the account says he withdrew into the grass. Others crouched or knelt to speak. A burned shoulder blade found in the ground can tell us that someone practised divination by bone. A body making room on a road leaves no comparable trace. Here an outsider gives us a gesture in which the whole difference of rank takes the time of a person passing.

Himiko was dealing with a form of recognition the mainland had offered before. In AD 57, an earlier Chinese history says, a ruler of Na received a seal and ribbon from the Han court. A tiny gold seal found on an island in Hakata Bay bears the title of the king of Na of Wa. A coiled snake forms the handle. The seal is small enough to close a hand around. Set down beside a jar or a bronze weapon, it shows a different sort of power at work in northern Kyushu more than a century before Himiko sent her envoys.

Himiko's envoys first came to the Chinese commandery of Daifang on the Korean peninsula and were sent on to the Wei court. The reply bestowed on her the title Queen of Wa Friendly to Wei, with a gold seal and a purple ribbon. The list of gifts included silks, swords and those hundred mirrors. The court instructed her to show the gifts to her people so they could see how Wei regarded her. An ornament laid beside a dead person tells us someone could afford to part with it. Here the words that travelled with the gifts tell us something else about bronze. The shine of a mirror could carry news of a queen's standing all the way from a court on the mainland.

The account gives a route in the other direction, from Daifang back into Wa. The stages through Tsushima and Iki and into northern Kyushu can be followed with some confidence. The people of one island lived on steep ground, with little to grow and much reason to cross the water for grain. Then comes the frustrating part. The directions, the turns and the sailing and walking times cease to fit together easily on a modern map. Read one way, the distances can carry the traveller on toward the Kinki and the Nara basin. Read another way, the record can be reconciled with a center in Kyushu. There are good archaeological reasons to take both regions seriously. A resemblance between the names Yamatai and Yamato is a clue that the uncertain route cannot settle.

When Himiko died, the Chinese account says, people raised a great mound more than a hundred paces across. It says more than a hundred enslaved people were made to die with her. A man took her place. The people refused to obey him, and the record puts the deaths in the fighting that followed at more than a thousand. Then a girl of thirteen from Himiko's clan became ruler. Her name was Iyo. Order returned, and envoys again went to the continent. The writer could name the woman and the girl and could tell what came to the court from across the water. We still cannot stand at a place on the ground and say with certainty that this was where either of them lived.

genealogy.caption: The male successor failed to secure obedience. Iyo, of Himiko’s clan, brought the succession crisis to an end in the Wei account.

paragraphs.text: The later Yamato court told a different story about the beginning of rule. In its eighth-century chronicles, the man later called Jimmu leaves southern Kyushu and travels east along the Inland Sea. At the approach to the country that will become his seat, his brother is wounded. The Kojiki makes the brother see the error in the way they have fought. They trace their descent to the sun goddess and have gone into battle facing her. They must go round and approach from the other side, with the sun at their backs. In the story, the journey south and around the Kii Peninsula turns a defeat into an approach sanctioned by their ancestry.

The court that set this journey down lived many centuries after the age to which it assigned Jimmu. Its route moves through real places, past the Inland Sea, Kibi and the difficult approaches to the Nara basin. It also moves through a world in which a goddess's descendants can ask the land to yield because of who they are. Some of the people who resist in the chronicles are called earth spiders. The name puts them outside the terms on which the future court recognizes rank and rightful resistance. We can learn something from that name about the people who used it. The communities it was meant to describe had their own names for themselves.

genealogy.caption: Sacred descent was the later court’s explanation for Jimmu’s right to rule.

paragraphs.text: Look back across the mountains to Izumo and the swords at Kojindani. In the chronicles, Izumo is the country where the exiled god Susa no O kills an eight-headed serpent beside the Hii River. His descendant Okuni Nushi, the god of many spears, must eventually yield the land to the heavenly line. He is promised a great dwelling and retains a sacred domain. A place that the court wishes to present as subordinate retains gods who have to be dealt with. The swords in the hillside belong to a different record. They allow us to see how much skill, metal and coordinated work people in Izumo commanded, without giving us the name of a chief.

genealogy.caption: Izumo’s sacred figures and the ancestral line of Yamato meet in the court’s story of the transfer of the land.

paragraphs.text: Later Japanese compilers did know of Chinese notices of a queen. The Nihon Shoki put notices of Wa's relations with Wei into the annals of the regent Jingu. That arrangement made the queen of the Chinese account readable within a much later Japanese line of succession. The differences persist. A reader can put the name Himiko beside Jingu and still find the girl Iyo, the younger brother, and the awkward itinerary to account for. The books from either side of the sea had different reasons for preserving what they did. For this part of the story, the gap between them is one of the things that has survived.

In the basin of Nara, something else begins to be visible in the third century. At Makimuku there was a concentration of buildings and material from several regions. In and around the basin, tombs took on a distinctive form. A round mound extended into a broad, angular forepart, making the outline we call a keyhole. Hashihaka is an immense early example. It has been proposed as Himiko's tomb. The scale, date and location make the proposal understandable, while the route in the Wei history remains unresolved and the mound has yielded no secure identification of its occupant.

Farther south near Tenri lies the great keyhole mound traditionally assigned to Sujin. The Kojiki says that Sujin first ruled the land, even though the received line puts nine rulers before him. The name of Sujin has stayed with the mound for centuries while the identity of the person buried there remains beyond reach. The mound is two hundred and forty-two metres long and probably took shape in the first half of the fourth century. Someone had to cut the earth and carry it, load by load, to make a hill in a shape already recognizable elsewhere. The emerging power in Yamato could put thousands of such small acts to one purpose. The earth still lies where the people who did the work left it.

genealogy.caption: The received dynasty puts Sujin tenth. The Kojiki calls him a beginning in his own right.
